name: Quantum Measurement Problem
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Moment of Truth: Why Measurement Changes Everything
lesson.summary: Covers what happens physically and mathematically when a qubit is measured, including the Born rule, the collapse of entangled states, and the open interpretational puzzle behind it.
lesson.body:
Superposition and entanglement, as described in the previous two sections, describe qubits before they are measured. Measurement is the process that connects the quantum description to an actual classical outcome you can read off an instrument, and it behaves in a way that is genuinely different from anything in classical physics. When you measure a qubit in the state alpha|0⟩ + beta|1⟩ in the standard basis, you do not learn alpha and beta. You get a single classical bit, 0 or 1, with probability |alpha| squared and |beta| squared respectively. This rule for turning amplitudes into probabilities is called the Born rule, and it is one of the foundational postulates of quantum mechanics.

Crucially, measurement is destructive to the superposition. Once you measure and get, say, 0, the qubit's state is now simply |0⟩. The information that used to be encoded in the relative size and phase of alpha and beta is gone, and measuring the same qubit again immediately afterward will just give 0 again with certainty. You cannot run the measurement once and somehow recover the original amplitudes from that single trial. This is why quantum algorithms are built around repeated runs and careful use of interference to make sure that, by the time measurement happens, the probability is concentrated heavily on the answer that is actually wanted, rather than spread thinly across many possibilities.

For entangled qubits, measurement has an additional consequence, as the entanglement section previewed. Measuring one half of an entangled pair collapses the entire joint state at once, fixing the outcome distribution for the other qubit even though it may be far away and untouched. As that section noted, this does not transmit usable information faster than light: the outcome on your side is random and only becomes a meaningful correlation once compared against the other side's result through an ordinary classical channel.

This is also where quantum mechanics has an unresolved conceptual puzzle, one that gives this section its name: the measurement problem. Away from measurement, quantum theory evolves smoothly and reversibly according to the Schrodinger equation. But measurement is described by an abrupt, seemingly irreversible jump, collapse from a superposition to one definite outcome, governed only by the Born rule's probabilities. Physicists disagree about why this jump happens and what, precisely, counts as a measurement. The Copenhagen interpretation simply takes collapse as a fundamental postulate. The many worlds interpretation avoids postulating collapse at all, treating every possible outcome as equally real in a larger, branching description. Decoherence, covered later in this book, explains much of why superpositions appear to vanish on interaction with a large environment, but it does not by itself settle why any one particular outcome is the one we experience.

For building and using a quantum computer, this interpretational debate can largely be set aside. Engineers use the measurement postulate operationally: prepare a state, evolve it through gates, measure it, and use the Born rule to predict outcome statistics across many runs. What matters practically is that measurement, intentional or not, destroys superposition and entanglement. Qubits must therefore be shielded from any interaction that could act like an accidental measurement while a computation is in progress, a requirement that is extraordinarily difficult to satisfy and is the direct cause of the fragility problems explored later in this book.
